newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia tugrik plummets on falling trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia tugrik plummets on falling trade surplus.

text.p: Mongolia's tugrik has fallen to 651.53 to the U.S. dollar from 473.62 earlier this year due in part to a shrinking trade surplus, officials and traders said on Thursday.
"One reason (for the tugrik's fall) is that the foreign currency flow from abroad to Mongolia has decreased," a spokesman for the Bank of Mongolia, the central bank, told Reuters.
"This is because the world market prices of Mongolia's main export items, copper and cashmere, have fallen while at the same time imports have been growing," he said.
Mongolia registered a trade surplus of $43.5 million in the first 10 months of 1996, down 49.2 percent from the same 1995 period, official figures show.
The spokesman said it was still impossible to predict when the tugrik would rebound.
One dollar bought 676 to 681 tugriks on the semi-official kerb market on Thursday but rates have hit as high as 690 this month, traders said.
Traders said the rates are also sensitive to the country's few international flights, before and after which there are often increases in the number of currency exchanges.
Most trading take place in the lively kerb market because most banks do not have the foreign currency reserves to handle large transactions, said one banker.
"People go to the street to change because the foreign exchange supplies in banks are small," said Nadmid, an official with the Commercial Trade and Development Bank.
